title: Operating Systems
description: Processes and threads, scheduling, synchronisation, deadlock, memory management and file systems. Scheduling and page-replacement answers are computed, not estimated.

questions.title: Process or thread?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a process and a thread? Why are threads called lightweight?
questions.answer:
A **process** is a program in execution with its **own address space** (code, heap, stack), open files and OS resources. A **thread** is a unit of execution **inside** a process: threads of one process **share** the code, heap and open files, but each has its own **stack, program counter and registers**.

Threads are lightweight because creating one and switching between threads of the same process is cheaper: no new address space, and no switch of page tables (and fewer TLB flushes). Communication is also cheaper (shared memory), but that sharing is why threads need synchronisation. Processes are isolated: one crashing does not corrupt another.

questions.title: What is a context switch?
questions.prompt: Describe a context switch and say why it is pure overhead.
questions.answer:
A context switch saves the state of the running process or thread (program counter, registers, stack pointer, and for processes the memory-management information) in its **process control block (PCB)** and loads the saved state of the next one chosen by the scheduler.

It is overhead because **no useful work** happens during it, and it has indirect costs too: the CPU caches and TLB hold the old process's data, so the new one suffers misses (a process switch costs more than a thread switch within one process because the address space changes). Too-short time slices therefore waste throughput.

questions.title: Average waiting time of scheduling algorithms
questions.prompt: Four processes arrive and need CPU bursts: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8, P2 at 1 with 4, P3 at 2 with 9, P4 at 3 with 5. Compute the average waiting time under FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and SRTF (preemptive SJF).
questions.answer:
Waiting time = completion time − arrival time − burst time.

- **FCFS** (order P1, P2, P3, P4): P1 0-8, P2 8-12, P3 12-21, P4 21-26. Waiting: 0, 7, 10, 18. Average = **8.75**.
- **SJF, non-preemptive:** P1 runs 0-8 (nothing else has arrived that is shorter when it starts); then the shortest ready job each time: P2 8-12, P4 12-17, P3 17-26. Waiting: 0, 7, 15, 9. Average = **7.75**.
- **SRTF** (preemptive): the process with the least remaining time always runs. Average = **6.5**.

SRTF gives the smallest average waiting time of the three, but it needs to know burst lengths in advance and can starve long jobs. Round robin with quantum 4 gives 11.75 on this input: fairer response times, worse average waiting.
questions.hint: Draw a Gantt chart. For waiting time use completion − arrival − burst.

questions.title: Choosing a scheduling algorithm
questions.prompt: Compare FCFS, SJF, Round Robin and priority scheduling. Which suits an interactive system?
questions.answer:
- **FCFS:** simple and fair in arrival order, but a long job delays everyone behind it (**convoy effect**).
- **SJF / SRTF:** minimises average waiting time, but needs burst predictions and can **starve** long jobs.
- **Round Robin:** each process gets a time **quantum** in turn: good **response time**, the usual choice for interactive systems. A quantum that is too large behaves like FCFS; one that is too small wastes time in context switches.
- **Priority:** the most important runs first; low-priority processes can starve, fixed by **aging** (raise priority with waiting time).

Real systems (Linux CFS, Windows) combine ideas: multilevel feedback queues with priorities, time slices and aging.

questions.title: Deadlock
questions.prompt: State the four necessary conditions for deadlock and explain how you can prevent it.
questions.answer:
Deadlock requires **all four**: (1) **mutual exclusion**: a resource is held by one process at a time; (2) **hold and wait**: a process holds resources while waiting for more; (3) **no preemption**: resources cannot be taken away; (4) **circular wait**: a cycle of processes each waiting for a resource held by the next.

**Prevention** breaks one condition: request all resources at once (breaks hold-and-wait); allow preemption; or impose a **global order** on resources and always acquire them in that order (breaks circular wait, the most practical). **Avoidance** (Banker's algorithm) grants a request only if the system stays in a safe state. **Detection and recovery** looks for cycles in the wait-for graph and kills or rolls back a process. Many systems simply ignore it and rely on timeouts.

questions.title: Mutex, semaphore and monitor
questions.prompt: What is a race condition? Compare a mutex, a semaphore and a monitor.
questions.answer:
A **race condition** happens when the result depends on the unpredictable interleaving of threads, typically two threads doing a read-modify-write on shared data (`count++` is load, add, store). The code that touches shared data is the **critical section**, which must be executed by one thread at a time (mutual exclusion).

- **Mutex (lock):** binary lock with an owner: only the thread that locked it may unlock it.
- **Semaphore:** an integer counter with atomic `wait` (P, decrement, blocking at 0) and `signal` (V, increment). A **counting** semaphore limits access to N identical resources; a binary semaphore resembles a mutex but has no owner and can be used for signalling between threads.
- **Monitor:** a language construct that bundles shared data, the procedures that use it and a lock, with **condition variables** (`wait`/`notify`). Java's `synchronized` with `wait/notify` is a monitor.

questions.title: Producer-consumer with semaphores
questions.prompt: Describe how to solve the bounded-buffer producer-consumer problem with semaphores.
questions.answer:
Use three semaphores for a buffer of size N: `empty = N` (free slots), `full = 0` (filled slots), and `mutex = 1` (protects the buffer structure).

```
Producer:  wait(empty); wait(mutex); add item; signal(mutex); signal(full)
Consumer:  wait(full);  wait(mutex); remove item; signal(mutex); signal(empty)
```

`empty` makes a producer block when the buffer is full and `full` makes a consumer block when it is empty. `mutex` keeps two threads from corrupting the buffer. **Order matters:** if a producer did `wait(mutex)` before `wait(empty)` and the buffer were full, it would sleep holding the mutex and the consumer could never get in: deadlock. In Java the same pattern is a `BlockingQueue`.

questions.title: Paging versus segmentation
questions.prompt: Compare paging and segmentation. What is internal and external fragmentation?
questions.answer:
**Paging** divides logical memory into fixed-size **pages** and physical memory into **frames** of the same size; a page table maps pages to frames. It removes external fragmentation and any page can go in any free frame, but the last page of a process wastes space (**internal fragmentation**, on average half a page).

**Segmentation** divides memory into variable-size **logical units** (code, stack, heap, a module) with a base and limit each. It matches the programmer's view and supports protection and sharing per segment, but suffers **external fragmentation**: free memory exists in many small holes between segments. Many systems combine them (paged segments).

**Internal fragmentation** = wasted space *inside* an allocated block. **External fragmentation** = free space that is split into pieces too small to use.

questions.title: Virtual memory and thrashing
questions.prompt: What is virtual memory and what is thrashing?
questions.answer:
**Virtual memory** lets a process use an address space larger than physical memory: only the pages in use (the **working set**) are in RAM and the rest stay on disk. A page-table entry marks a page absent; touching it causes a **page fault**, the OS loads the page (replacing another if needed) and restarts the instruction. Benefits: programs bigger than RAM, process isolation, simple memory sharing, on-demand loading.

**Thrashing** occurs when processes do not have enough frames for their working sets, so they fault constantly and the system spends most of its time moving pages instead of computing: CPU utilisation collapses. Remedies: reduce the multiprogramming level, give each process enough frames (working-set or page-fault-frequency policies), or add RAM.

questions.title: Page replacement
questions.prompt: For the reference string [7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2] with 3 frames, count the page faults for FIFO, LRU and the optimal policy.
questions.answer:
- **FIFO** evicts the oldest page: **10** faults.
- **LRU** evicts the least recently used page: **9** faults.
- **Optimal** evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future: **7** faults (the minimum possible; it needs knowledge of the future, so it is used only as a benchmark).

FIFO can suffer **Belady's anomaly** (more frames, more faults). LRU and OPT are **stack algorithms** and never do. LRU is approximated in practice with a reference bit (the clock or second-chance algorithm), because exact LRU is expensive to track.
questions.hint: Keep the frame contents after every reference and mark each fault.

questions.title: System calls and kernel mode
questions.prompt: What is a system call? Why does the CPU have user mode and kernel mode?
questions.answer:
A **system call** is the controlled entry point through which a user program asks the kernel to do something privileged: read a file, create a process, allocate memory, send a network packet (`read`, `write`, `fork`, `mmap`). The program executes a special instruction (a **trap**) which switches the CPU to **kernel mode**, runs the kernel routine, and returns to user mode.

Two modes protect the system: in **user mode** a program cannot execute privileged instructions (I/O, changing page tables, disabling interrupts) or touch kernel memory, so a buggy or malicious program cannot crash the machine or read other programs' data. Only the kernel runs in kernel mode.

questions.title: fork, exec, zombie and orphan
questions.prompt: Explain `fork()` and `exec()`. What are zombie and orphan processes?
questions.answer:
`fork()` creates a **child** that is a copy of the parent (copy-on-write makes it cheap); it returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. `exec()` **replaces** the current process image with a new program. A shell runs a command by `fork()` then `exec()` in the child while the parent `wait()`s.

A **zombie** is a process that has terminated but whose parent has not yet called `wait()` to read its exit status: it keeps only a process-table entry. An **orphan** is a process whose parent has terminated; the init/systemd process adopts it. A pile of zombies means the parent never reaps its children.

questions.title: Inodes and file systems
questions.prompt: In a Unix-like file system, what is an inode and what is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?
questions.answer:
An **inode** stores a file's **metadata** (owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count) and pointers to its **data blocks** (direct pointers, then single, double and triple indirect blocks for large files), but **not the file name**. A directory is a table mapping names to inode numbers.

A **hard link** is another directory entry pointing to the **same inode**: the file data is deleted only when the link count reaches zero, and hard links cannot cross file systems or point to directories. A **symbolic (soft) link** is a small file containing a **path**; it can cross file systems and point to directories, but it **dangles** if the target is removed.

questions.title: Interrupts and the kernel
questions.prompt: What happens when an interrupt occurs while a process is running?
questions.answer: The hardware finishes the current instruction, saves the program counter and flags, switches to kernel mode and jumps through the **interrupt vector table** to the **interrupt service routine (ISR)**. The ISR handles the device (read the data, acknowledge) as quickly as possible, often only queueing the work, and then returns from the interrupt. The scheduler may then choose a different process, so an interrupt such as a timer tick is also how **preemptive multitasking** happens. Interrupts come from devices; **exceptions/traps** come from the running instruction (page fault, divide by zero, system call).

questions.title: Containers versus virtual machines
questions.prompt: How is a container different from a virtual machine?
questions.answer: A **virtual machine** emulates hardware with a **hypervisor** and runs a **complete guest OS** with its own kernel: strong isolation, heavy (GBs, minutes to boot). A **container** is an ordinary process (or group) on the host kernel, isolated with **namespaces** (own view of processes, network, mounts) and limited with **cgroups** (CPU, memory, I/O): lightweight (MBs, starts in a second) and dense, but all containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability affects them all and a container cannot run a different OS kernel. Docker packages an application with its dependencies into an image that runs the same on any host with a compatible kernel.
